name: Hair dye / bleaching hair
lead: Hair dyeing and bleaching change the colour of scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair with chemical colourants or lighteners. In looksmaxxing communities they are discussed as ways to adjust contrast, cover grey, darken sparse eyebrows or beard, or change overall look [1][2].

Dyes are classed by permanence: permanent dyes use ammonia and a peroxide developer and can lighten, while semi-permanent and temporary dyes deposit colour without lightening [3]. The main documented harm is allergic contact dermatitis, especially to para-phenylenediamine (PPD), and cancer associations remain debated [3][4].

paras: Wikipedia describes permanent dyes as containing ammonia that opens the hair cuticle so dye reaches the cortex, mixed with hydrogen peroxide developer; demi-permanent dyes deposit colour without lightening and fade over about 20 to 28 shampoos; semi-permanent dyes last about 4 to 8 shampoos; temporary pigments rinse out with one wash [3].

Bleaching breaks down melanin by oxidation, using hydrogen peroxide with alkaline ammonia; home products typically use about 6% peroxide and salon products up to 12%, and bleached hair can turn brassy, which toners or purple shampoo counter [3].

Wikipedia traces hair colouring to ancient recipes such as those in the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE), William Henry Perkin's discovery of the first synthetic dye in 1856, L'Oreal founder Eugene Schueller's first synthetic hair dye in 1907, and Schwarzkopf's first home colour product in 1947 [3].

PPD-based dyes are the main allergen concern; reactions include redness, itching, burning and sores, sometimes appearing hours to a day later [3]. Reviews cover allergic contact dermatitis to cosmetics and PPD sensitisation, and a Danish study followed hairdressing apprentices for hand eczema [4][5][6]. A study found the consumer open test can detect contact sensitivity to hair dyes [7], and Wikipedia notes European dermatologists have advised against self-patch-testing because it may increase sensitisation risk [3].

Cancer evidence is mixed. A 1975 study found hair dyes contained mutagenic ingredients, and a 2004 review addressed toxicity and human health risk of hair dyes [8][9]. Wikipedia says the IARC considers some dyes and ingredients mutagenic or carcinogenic but that evidence linking use to cancer is limited and inconsistent, citing meta-analyses suggesting roughly 20% higher breast cancer risk among users [3].
Wikipedia reports that the EU restricts about 45 chemicals in hair dyes under its cosmetics directives [3]. A cosmetic ingredient safety assessment of Basic Red 76 has also been published [10].

A multicentre clinical trial studied a permanent dye containing paratoluenediamine, and a clinical study tested a gallic acid-based dye in patients reactive to PPD or PTD [11][12]. A PPD-specific lymphocyte activation test has been evaluated in sensitised patients [13]. No studies were found on dyeing as a looksmaxxing practice.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair dye threads cover colour choice, natural dyes and using dye on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair [1][2][14].

claims.claim: Dye on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair improves how dark and full they look
claims.believers: A thread discusses hair dye working on eyebrows, lashes and facial hair for darker-haired users [14].
claims.experts: Allergic contact dermatitis to dye ingredients is documented, and Wikipedia notes European dermatologists advise against self patch tests [3][4].

claims.claim: Natural dyes are a safer alternative
claims.believers: Users ask about the best natural hair dye [15].
claims.experts: A gallic acid-based dye was tested on patients reactive to PPD and PTD in one study [12]; no study evaluates forum natural-dye recommendations.

card.summary: Dyeing or bleaching hair for colour and contrast; common cosmetic practice with documented allergy risk.
card.note: PPD allergy can be severe; bleaching peroxide can damage hair and skin.

quick.overview:
Hair dyeing and bleaching change hair colour using chemical colourants or lighteners. Looksmaxxers use them for hair, brows and facial hair.

The chemistry is well documented. Research on harms centres on allergy, with mixed evidence on cancer.
quick.mechanism: Permanent dyes use ammonia and peroxide to open the cuticle and form colour in the hair; bleach oxidises melanin. Semi-permanent and temporary dyes coat or sit under the cuticle and wash out.
quick.risks: PPD allergy can cause itching, burning and sores, sometimes delayed. IARC lists some ingredients as mutagenic or carcinogenic, though overall evidence linking dye use to cancer is described as limited and inconsistent. The EU restricts many dye chemicals.
